Launch private-label retail products (D2C + in-salon) for high-margin revenue
Open clinical/advanced verticals (skin, hair-loss, slimming) under medical supervision
Build a loyalty + app ecosystem and explore Tier-2/3 expansion where rents are lower

kpi_structure.definition: Booked productive hours divided by available stylist-chair hours
Share of clients who return within 90 days
Total bill per client visit (service + retail)
Product retail revenue as % of service revenue
Booked appointments not honoured
Service revenue generated per active stylist per month

playbooks.one_liner: An Indian beauty and wellness MSME — salons, spas, skin/hair clinics and cosmetic-service outlets — that sells skilled appointment-based services plus retail products, monetised through walk-ins, memberships and packages.

operating_model.summary: A high-fixed-cost, footfall-and-skill-driven service business where profit is made by keeping skilled stylist-chairs occupied at a healthy ticket size, converting one-time visitors into members and adding high-margin retail and clinical services. Cash flow benefits from prepaid memberships but is squeezed by rent, attrition-prone skilled labour and consumable inventory.
revenue_streams: Walk-in and booked services (hair, skin, beauty, grooming, massage/spa)
Memberships and prepaid service packages (advance cash float)
Retail product sales (in-salon and D2C/private-label)
Bridal, event and home-service packages
Clinical/advanced treatments (skin, hair-loss, slimming) under medical supervision
Training academy fees and franchise royalties (at scale)
cost_structure: Rent and fit-out amortisation (often 18-30% of revenue, esp. Tier-1 malls/high-streets)
Skilled labour: stylist salary + commission/incentive (30-40% of revenue)
Consumables and retail COGS (colour, wax, serums, linen, disposables)
Marketing and aggregator commissions (Urban Company etc. take 20-30%)
Utilities (power, water heating), licences, software/POS and card/UPI charges
value_drivers: Skilled stylist talent retention and productivity
Chair utilisation and repeat-visit frequency
Membership penetration and retail attach-rate
Brand reputation, hygiene standards and local reviews
Location footfall quality and rent-to-revenue ratio

operational_bottlenecks.symptom: Top stylists leave and take their client following with them; constant rehiring and retraining
operational_bottlenecks.impact: Revenue volatility, broken client relationships, quality inconsistency
operational_bottlenecks.root_cause: Stylist-owned (not salon-owned) client relationships, low base pay reliant on commission, and a thin pool of trained talent in India

operational_bottlenecks.symptom: Empty chairs on weekday mornings, overbooked and turning clients away on weekends/evenings
operational_bottlenecks.impact: Low utilisation drags margin while peak demand is lost
operational_bottlenecks.root_cause: Footfall concentrated in evenings/weekends/festive season with fixed staffing and no dynamic pricing or rostering

operational_bottlenecks.symptom: 15-25% of booked slots wasted with no reminder discipline
operational_bottlenecks.impact: Direct loss of irrecoverable stylist-hour capacity
operational_bottlenecks.root_cause: Manual diary booking, no deposit/confirmation flow, and absent automated reminders

operational_bottlenecks.bottleneck: Cash leakage and weak POS discipline
operational_bottlenecks.symptom: Unbilled services, off-the-book cash, untracked discounts and commission disputes
operational_bottlenecks.impact: Profit erosion, GST exposure and inability to trust the numbers
operational_bottlenecks.root_cause: Cash-heavy culture, manual billing and no enforced POS-per-transaction control

operational_bottlenecks.symptom: Stockouts of hero colours/products mid-service and dead stock of slow movers
operational_bottlenecks.impact: Lost services, working-capital tied up, expiry write-offs
operational_bottlenecks.root_cause: No SKU-level tracking, eyeball reordering and free use of products without per-service costing

operational_bottlenecks.symptom: Heavy reliance on Urban Company/Yes Madam for bookings at 20-30% commission
operational_bottlenecks.impact: Thin margins and no ownership of the client relationship
operational_bottlenecks.root_cause: Weak own-channel acquisition and CRM, so the platform owns the customer

pm_workflows.cadence: One-time, 90-120 day project with weekly steering reviews
milestones: Licences secured (Shops Act, trade, Drugs cosmetics, fire NOC)
Hiring + SOP training of stylist team
Soft launch with membership pre-sell, then grand opening

pm_workflows.cadence: 6-8 week build, then always-on monthly optimisation
milestones: Define tiers, pricing and breakage assumptions
Configure in POS/CRM and train front-desk on the pitch
Review penetration, redemption and retention monthly
Supplier + formulation selection and BIS/Drugs-Cosmetics compliance
Staff retail-selling training and attach-rate targets

key_activities: Client consultation and patch-test where required
Hygienic, SOP-driven service by assigned stylist
POS billing with GST invoice and digital payment
Automated reminders and win-back for lapsed clients
Move client up to memberships, packages, clinical add-ons
Cross-sell across outlets and D2C retail

profitability_analysis.typical_gross_margin: 55-70% (service revenue after consumables and direct product COGS)
profitability_analysis.typical_net_margin: 8-18% at a mature single outlet; new outlets often loss-making for 6-12 months
unit_economics: Per-chair: a productive stylist-chair targets ₹1.5-3 lakh/month revenue; break-even occupancy is roughly 45-55% of available hours
Average ticket ₹900-2,500; consumable cost 12-20% of service price; stylist commission 8-15% of the bill
Membership float: a ₹15,000 annual package collected upfront funds 3-6 months of working capital at near-zero cost
CAC ₹150-600 per new client via own channel vs effective 20-30% give-up on aggregator-acquired clients
profitability_analysis.working_capital_notes: Structurally favourable due to prepaid memberships/packages (negative working capital) and instant UPI/card settlement; the drains are consumable inventory, rent deposits (6-12 months) and fit-out capex. Watch Sec 43B(h): pay MSME product/consumable suppliers within 45 days or lose the expense deduction.
levers: Lift chair utilisation in trough hours via off-peak pricing and rostering
Raise retail attach-rate from sub-5% toward 12-18%
Grow membership penetration to lock in repeat revenue and float
Shift acquisition from aggregators to own CRM to recover the 20-30% commission
Tie stylist pay to productivity and retail attach to align incentives

risk_model.risk: Operating without valid Shops & Establishment / trade licence and labour registrations
risk_model.control: Maintain a licence calendar; register under Shops Act, EPFO/ESIC once thresholds are met, and renew on time

risk_model.risk: Selling/applying non-compliant cosmetics or skin/hair products (mislabelled, unregistered, banned ingredients)
risk_model.control: Source only Drugs-and-Cosmetics-Act compliant, BIS-marked products; keep supplier certificates and avoid grey-market imports

risk_model.risk: Clinical/adverse-event liability (burns, allergic reactions, botched treatments) and unsupervised medical procedures
risk_model.control: Mandatory patch-tests and consent forms, trained-only-staff SOPs, doctor supervision for clinical services, and professional-indemnity insurance

risk_model.risk: GST and cash-billing exposure across service + retail with multi-outlet POS
risk_model.control: Enforce POS-per-transaction billing, e-invoice/GST reconciliation, and correct rate classification for services vs goods

risk_model.risk: Wage, PF/ESI and labour-code non-compliance for stylists and therapists
risk_model.control: Formal contracts, payroll with EPFO/ESIC/PT deductions, and adherence to the new labour codes on wages and conditions

risk_model.risk: FSSAI breach where wellness/spa sells ingestibles, teas, supplements or in-cafe items
risk_model.control: Obtain FSSAI licence/registration before selling any consumable and follow labelling norms

risk_model.risk: Delayed payments to MSME consumable/product suppliers triggering Sec 43B(h) disallowance
risk_model.control: Pay registered MSME suppliers within 45 days; track Udyam status of vendors in the payables system

value_chain: Demand generation (local SEO, reviews, aggregators, referrals)

core_processes.description: Booking, confirmation, reminders and stylist rostering to maximise chair utilisation and minimise no-shows
Standardised hygiene, sterilisation, consultation and treatment protocols ensuring consistent, safe outcomes across stylists and outlets
POS-enforced billing, digital payment, discount governance and GST/e-invoice reconciliation across service and retail lines
SKU-level consumable and retail stock tracking, per-service costing, reorder points and compliant supplier sourcing
Client database, RFM segmentation, membership/package management and automated reactivation campaigns

playbooks.name: Furniture Businesses

ai_automation_opportunities.opportunity: Auto-generate quotations from a parametric BOM (board sq.ft, hardware, laminate, edge-banding, labour) so showroom/site staff issue priced quotes in minutes instead of the owner hand-calculating each night, cutting quote-to-order time and stopping under-quoting of carcass/hardware

Job-card / WIP tracker that tags each order through cutting -> edge-banding -> assembly -> polish -> dispatch, flagging stalled jobs and giving the owner a live shop-floor board instead of chasing the karigar verbally

Plywood/laminate/hardware reorder agent on min-max levels with mandi/dealer price tracking, so fast-moving SKUs (18mm ply, common laminates, hinges, channels) never stock out and slow dead stock is liquidated
GST e-invoice + e-way bill automation for B2B/contractor orders and inter-state showroom dispatch, classifying HSN 9403 (furniture) vs 4412 (ply) at correct rates and avoiding transit detention
AI room-visualiser / catalogue render from a customer photo + dimensions to show modular kitchen/wardrobe options at the showroom, lifting close rate and average ticket without a designer present
Site-measurement-to-cutting-list converter that turns a measurement sheet into an optimised panel cutting layout (nesting) to reduce board wastage from ~15-20% toward 8-10%
Receivables follow-up agent for contractor/builder/B2B credit accounts: auto-reminders, ageing buckets, and Sec 43B(h) MSME-payment monitoring on what the firm owes its own MSME suppliers

consulting_frameworks.use: The polish/finishing booth and skilled karigar bandwidth are the chronic bottleneck in a furniture unit; TOC schedules all upstream cutting/assembly to the throughput of finishing, exposing where to add a second polish line or outsource

Map margin and lead-time across procure (ply/laminate/hardware) -> design/measure -> cut/edge-band -> assemble -> finish -> deliver/install, to see where wastage and rework destroy the 30-40% gross margin

Furniture ties cash in raw board inventory + long WIP + builder/contractor receivables; modelling inventory days + WIP days + DSO minus supplier credit reveals the real cash gap funding each ₹1 of growth

Cost a modular kitchen or wardrobe per running-foot / per sq.ft of board: material + hardware + labour + finishing + delivery/install vs price, to set a defensible price list and kill loss-making custom jobs

Customers hire furniture for 'fit my space, on a date, that lasts' — clarifies why on-time delivery, finish quality and warranty beat raw price for the home-owner segment vs lowest-rate for the contractor segment
Defines who is Responsible/Accountable for site measurement vs cutting list vs final dimensions — the single biggest source of costly remakes is unclear ownership of the measurement-to-cut handoff

department_structure.mandate: Convert walk-ins, architects, contractors and online enquiries into priced orders; capture accurate measurements, designs and customer expectations
Convert cutting lists into finished furniture on time and within material norms: cutting, edge-banding, assembly, finishing/polish
Source ply, MDF, laminate, hardware, adhesives and consumables at best rate/credit; maintain min-max stock and issue material against job cards
Pack, transport, install on site, handle snags and warranty service to protect reviews and referrals
Billing, GST e-invoice/e-way, advances vs balance collection, receivables, payroll, statutory filings

digital_maturity_model.name: Manual / paper
signals: Quotes scribbled in a notebook or on WhatsApp
Cutting lists from memory; no written job card
Stock checked by eye; reorders when shelf looks empty
Receivables tracked in a diary
Bills handwritten, GST done monthly by the CA from a bag of slips
digital_maturity_model.next_step: Move quotations and order register into a structured spreadsheet/Tally with a standard SKU and rate list

digital_maturity_model.name: Digitised records
signals: Tally/Busy for billing and GST; spreadsheet order register
Standardised rate card and laminate/hardware catalogue
WhatsApp Business for enquiries with saved catalogue
Basic stock register in Excel
Photos of finished work stored for reference
digital_maturity_model.next_step: Adopt a quoting + job-card tool that links each order to a BOM and shop-floor stage

digital_maturity_model.name: Integrated workflow
signals: Parametric quotation tool generating BOM and price
Job cards tracked stage-wise (cut->polish->dispatch)
Min-max inventory with reorder alerts
GST e-invoice/e-way auto-generated from billing
Receivables ageing visible by customer
digital_maturity_model.next_step: Connect design/measurement to an automated cutting/nesting list and capture material-wastage data

digital_maturity_model.name: Data-driven operations
signals: Nesting/optimisation cuts board wastage to single digits
Dashboards on margin per order, on-time delivery, rework %
Demand forecast drives ply/laminate purchasing
Online catalogue/visualiser feeding showroom close rate
Karigar productivity and finishing throughput measured
digital_maturity_model.next_step: Layer AI on top: auto-quoting from a room photo, predictive reorder, and AI scheduling against the finishing constraint

digital_maturity_model.name: AI-native
signals: Customer photo + dimensions -> instant rendered design and priced quote
AI nesting + AI production scheduling around the polish bottleneck
Predictive procurement on price and lead-time signals
Automated receivables and Sec 43B(h) supplier-payment monitoring
Continuous margin and wastage analytics steering the price list
digital_maturity_model.next_step: Sustain with periodic model retraining on local order data and expand to multi-showroom orchestration

stages.focus: Stabilise quality and delivery; standardise rate card; win local home-owners and small contractors
plays: Build a fixed rate card per running-foot and stop free-handing quotes
Get Udyam + GST and start issuing proper invoices to unlock B2B/contractor orders
Collect 40-50% advance to fund material and protect cash
Photograph every job and run a Google Business + WhatsApp catalogue for referrals

stages.focus: Move from job-work to a branded showroom with repeatable modular products; tighten WIP and wastage
plays: Open/upgrade a showroom with display kitchens and wardrobes; tie up with 10-20 architects/interior designers
Introduce parametric quoting + job cards; measure margin per order and on-time delivery
Add panel-saw/edge-bander to cut wastage and dependence on individual karigars
Formalise a credit policy with ageing buckets; separate home-owner (advance) vs B2B (credit) terms

stages.focus: Scale capacity and brand; add e-commerce/marketplace and multi-city distribution; institutionalise systems
plays: Standardise SKUs for online/marketplace (Pepperfry, Amazon, own D2C) alongside custom
Run multiple showrooms/dealers with central production and ERP-driven planning
Invest in nesting/automation and a second finishing line to break the polish constraint
Pursue contractor/institutional and project (hotel/office fit-out) tenders with RERA-aware site documentation

kpi_structure.definition: (Selling price - material - hardware - direct labour - finishing - delivery) / selling price, per order
Wasted/offcut board value as a share of board consumed
Orders delivered and installed by the committed date
Share of jobs requiring remake or major rework (usually wrong measurement or finish defect)
Average days to collect from credit customers (builders/contractors/institutions)
Days from order confirmation to dispatch for a standard kitchen/wardrobe
Orders booked / qualified showroom and online enquiries

playbooks.one_liner: An Indian furniture MSME designs, manufactures (woodwork/carpentry, modular ply-and-laminate), and sells through showroom retail, contractors/architects and increasingly online — typically custom-plus-modular kitchens, wardrobes and home/office furniture made in a small workshop or organised unit.

operating_model.summary: A make-to-order plus make-to-stock business: customers (home-owners, architects/interior designers, contractors, and institutions) place custom or modular orders that are produced in-house from plywood/MDF, laminate, veneer and hardware, then delivered and installed. Revenue is driven by ticket size and conversion at the showroom/site, while profit is decided by material wastage, karigar productivity, and how fast cash is recovered against long WIP and contractor credit.
revenue_streams: Custom & modular furniture orders (kitchens, wardrobes, beds, sofas, office furniture) priced per running-foot/sq.ft
Showroom retail sale of ready/branded furniture and display pieces
Contractor / builder / architect channel and project fit-outs (hotels, offices, hostels)
Installation, polishing/refurbishing and repair/warranty service
Online/marketplace sales (own D2C site, Pepperfry/Amazon/Flipkart) of standard SKUs
cost_structure: Raw material: plywood/MDF/particle board, laminate/veneer, adhesives, hardware (hinges, channels, handles) — 45-60% of order cost
Direct labour: carpenters/karigars, polishers, fitters (often piece-rate or contract)
Finishing & consumables: PU/melamine polish, edge-band, sandpaper, screws
Showroom rent, display inventory and electricity/power for machines
Delivery, transport (e-way) and installation crew
Overheads: GST/compliance, statutory (EPF/ESI/PT), interest on working capital, marketing
value_drivers: Finish quality and on-time delivery (drives referrals and B2B repeat orders)
Material yield / low wastage from good cutting & nesting
Skilled karigar retention and finishing throughput
Design and quoting speed at the point of sale
Cash discipline: advances collected and contractor receivables controlled

operational_bottlenecks.bottleneck: Wrong site measurements causing costly remakes
operational_bottlenecks.symptom: Wardrobes/kitchens don't fit on installation; panels remade, delivery slips, customer angry
operational_bottlenecks.impact: Direct margin loss (material + labour redone), delayed payment, reputation damage
operational_bottlenecks.root_cause: Unclear ownership of the measure-to-cut handoff and no standardised measurement sheet/sign-off (RACI gap); the person measuring is not the person cutting

operational_bottlenecks.bottleneck: High plywood/board wastage and unoptimised cutting
operational_bottlenecks.symptom: Offcuts pile up; material cost overruns the quote; 15-20% board wasted
operational_bottlenecks.impact: Erodes already thin gross margin and inflates working capital tied in scrap
operational_bottlenecks.root_cause: Manual cutting without nesting/optimisation and no per-order material reconciliation against a BOM

operational_bottlenecks.symptom: Jobs pile up at the polish booth; everything else finishes but orders dispatch late
operational_bottlenecks.impact: Long WIP, missed delivery dates, cash stuck in near-finished goods
operational_bottlenecks.root_cause: Production scheduled by cutting/assembly capacity, not by the slower finishing/drying stage; single polish line and few skilled finishers

operational_bottlenecks.symptom: Quality and output swing with which karigar is present; work stalls when a key man leaves or takes leave
operational_bottlenecks.impact: Inconsistent finish, delivery risk, inability to scale beyond the owner's personal supervision
operational_bottlenecks.root_cause: Tacit, person-dependent skill with no written SOPs, jigs or standardisation; informal piece-rate labour with weak retention

operational_bottlenecks.symptom: Big B2B orders booked but payment delayed 60-120 days; owner borrows to buy next lot of ply
operational_bottlenecks.impact: Cash crunch despite full order book; growth self-funded by costly working capital
operational_bottlenecks.root_cause: Weak credit policy and no ageing discipline; market norm of credit to contractors with no documented terms or retention milestones

operational_bottlenecks.symptom: Order looks profitable but loses money after hardware, finishing and rework are counted
operational_bottlenecks.impact: Negative-margin jobs hidden inside a busy workshop; owner can't tell winners from losers
operational_bottlenecks.root_cause: Quotes built from memory/feel rather than a parametric BOM; hardware and finishing under-counted

milestones: Define SKU list and per-running-foot rates
Build BOM template (board, laminate, hardware, labour, finishing)
Pilot on next 20 quotes vs old method
Lock price list and train showroom/site staff
Run a physical/board pilot on one line
Add stage timestamps and stalled-job flags
Review WIP and on-time delivery weekly
Set advance policy (40-50%) and B2B credit terms
Build receivables ageing buckets by customer
Introduce reminders and retention milestones for projects
Track DSO and inventory days monthly
Introduce a cutting/nesting layout step before cutting
Reconcile material per order against BOM

key_activities: Understand space, budget and finish expectations
Collect advance and confirm delivery date
Raise order and release to production
Procure/issue board, laminate, hardware against job card
Pack and dispatch with e-way bill

unit_economics: Modular kitchen: ~₹1,200-2,500 per running-foot to customer; material+hardware ~₹650-1,400/rft, labour+finishing ~₹250-450/rft, leaving ~30-40% gross
Sliding wardrobe (8x7 ft, ~56 sq.ft): selling ~₹85,000-1,40,000; board+laminate+hardware ~₹45,000-70,000; gross ~₹30,000-50,000 per unit
Showroom enquiry-to-order conversion of 20-30% on an average ticket of ₹60,000-1,50,000 (home modular) drives revenue per walk-in
profitability_analysis.working_capital_notes: Cash is tied in three places at once: raw board/laminate/hardware inventory (15-30 days), long WIP through finishing (15-30 days), and contractor/builder receivables (45-90+ days). Home-owner advances of 40-50% partly fund this; B2B/project work runs cash-negative until milestone collection, so DSO control and supplier credit (watch Sec 43B(h) on MSME suppliers) decide survivability.
levers: Cut board wastage from ~18% toward ~10% via nesting — direct margin gain on the largest cost line
Shift mix toward higher-margin modular SKUs and finishing/upgrade add-ons vs pure low-rate contract job-work
Raise advances and tighten contractor DSO to slash working-capital interest
Break the finishing constraint (second polish line/outsource) to lift throughput without proportional overhead
Standardise SOPs/jigs to reduce rework and karigar dependence, protecting both margin and delivery

risk_model.risk: Customer/contractor payment default or long delays on credit sales
risk_model.control: Advance + milestone collection, documented credit terms, ageing reviews, retention only against sign-off

risk_model.risk: Volatile plywood/laminate/hardware prices and supply
risk_model.control: Min-max stock on fast movers, multi-vendor sourcing, lock rates for project quotes, pass-through clauses

risk_model.risk: Skilled karigar attrition / labour dependence
risk_model.control: Written SOPs and jigs, cross-training, retention incentives, EPF/ESI compliance to formalise workforce

risk_model.risk: BIS/quality non-conformity on boards and furniture (formaldehyde, ply grade) and product liability
risk_model.control: Source BIS-marked ply/board, maintain grade certificates, define QC checklist and warranty terms

risk_model.risk: GST e-invoice / e-way bill errors causing transit detention or ITC denial
risk_model.control: Automate e-invoice and e-way generation, correct HSN (9403 furniture vs 4412 ply) and rates, reconcile ITC

risk_model.risk: Factory/fire and labour-law non-compliance (dust, polish solvents, machinery)
risk_model.control: Factory licence and fire NOC, dust extraction and PPE, machine guarding, shops/labour-code registrations

risk_model.risk: Working-capital crunch despite a full order book
risk_model.control: Cash-flow forecasting, advance discipline, WIP reduction, RBI-MSME credit lines for the cash gap

risk_model.risk: Project/builder fit-out exposure to delayed real-estate projects
risk_model.control: Verify RERA-registered projects, stage-link payments to construction milestones, limit single-project exposure

value_chain: Procurement & material issue against job card

core_processes.description: Standardised site-measurement sheet signed off and converted into an optimised cutting/nesting list, with clear ownership to prevent remakes
Confirmed orders released as job cards and scheduled against the finishing constraint, tracked stage-by-stage to protect on-time delivery
Min-max reorder on ply/laminate/hardware and BOM-based issue per job, with per-order material reconciliation to control wastage
Parametric quote -> advance -> GST e-invoice -> dispatch e-way bill -> balance collection -> receivables ageing for B2B credit

playbooks.name: Hardware Stores
playbooks.one_liner: A neighbourhood/Tier-2/3 retail-cum-counter business selling building materials, paints, electricals, plumbing, sanitaryware, fasteners and tools to masons, contractors, electricians, plumbers and walk-in homeowners, run on credit relationships, dealer/distributor beats and deep SKU breadth.

operating_model.summary: Owner-operated counter retail with a high-SKU, low-shelf-life-risk inventory (cement, paints, pipes, wires, switches, fasteners, sanitaryware, tools, adhesives). Revenue splits between cash walk-ins (homeowners) and credit-based trade buyers (contractors, plumbers, electricians, masons). Margins are made through distributor schemes/slabs, brand incentives and quarterly target rebates rather than sticker markup. Working capital is the real business: inventory turns plus trade-credit float decide survival.
revenue_streams: Counter cash sales to walk-in homeowners and small jobs (paints, fittings, tools, hardware)
Credit sales to trade accounts (contractors, builders, plumbers, electricians) on 15-60 day terms
Project/bulk supply to small builders and civil contractors at thin margin but high volume
Brand/distributor schemes, slab discounts, quarterly target rebates and display/POSM incentives
Value-add services: paint tinting (computerised colour machines), key cutting, pipe threading, home delivery
cost_structure: Inventory purchase (COGS) = 78-86% of revenue; the dominant cost line
Trade credit float / interest cost on working-capital limits (CC/OD) or informal financing
Shop rent (high-street/market frontage) + electricity + power-backup
Staff: counter sales boys, loader/helper, delivery, accountant; often family labour
Shrinkage, breakage (sanitaryware/tiles), dead/slow-moving stock write-down, and bad debts on trade credit
value_drivers: SKU breadth + fill-rate: the shop that has the exact size/brand the contractor needs wins the order
Trade-credit relationships and recovery discipline (the moat AND the risk)
Buying power: distributor slabs, scheme capture and direct-from-company deals on fast movers
Location/catchment density of construction activity and number of loyal trade accounts
Inventory turns and dead-stock control that convert shelf space into cash

value_chain: Demand sensing (construction activity, contractor pipeline, seasonal/festive paint demand)
Procurement & assortment (distributor beats, company direct, scheme capture, reorder)
Inbound, GRN & stock-keeping (binning by category, batch/MRP/HSN tagging)
Counter sales & quotation (walk-in + trade order taking, price negotiation)
Billing, GST invoicing & credit decisioning (cash vs khata vs trade credit)
Fulfilment & last-mile (counter pickup, home/site delivery, loading)
Receivables management & collection (khata recovery, ageing follow-up)
Brand reconciliation (scheme/rebate claims, returns, warranty handling)

core_processes.description: Min/max or visual reorder against distributor van/beat schedules; balancing fast movers (cement, wire, white cement, PVC) vs long-tail SKUs; capturing brand schemes without over-stocking dead lines.
Deciding credit limit per contractor, recording udhaar (often in paper bahi-khata or basic Tally), invoicing on GST, and chasing ageing receivables before they turn into bad debt.
Issuing tax invoices with correct HSN and slab (cement 28%, paints 18%, many hardware items 18%), claiming input tax credit against purchase invoices, and reconciling GSTR-2B vs purchase register.
Physical stock counts, dead-stock identification, breakage/return handling for tiles/sanitaryware, and matching physical stock to book stock to control leakage.

department_structure.mandate: Convert walk-ins and trade orders, quote accurately, upsell allied SKUs, maintain product knowledge across paints/electrical/plumbing/hardware.
Run distributor beats, capture schemes, place reorders, do GRN, control dead stock and shrinkage, manage warehouse/godown binning.
GST invoicing, cash/UPI reconciliation, Tally bookkeeping, ITC matching, khata/receivables ledger, statutory filings.
Loading, home/site delivery, vehicle scheduling, e-way bill for bulk/inter-city dispatch, breakage-safe handling.

operational_bottlenecks.symptom: Cash tied up in contractor khatas for 45-90+ days; owner borrows to restock while customers owe lakhs.
operational_bottlenecks.impact: Working-capital starvation, inability to buy on scheme, reliance on costly informal credit, periodic bad-debt write-offs.
operational_bottlenecks.root_cause: Credit extended on relationship/trust without limits, ageing visibility or recovery discipline; contractors themselves paid late by builders/clients.

operational_bottlenecks.bottleneck: Dead and slow-moving stock across a long SKU tail
operational_bottlenecks.symptom: Godown full of odd sizes, discontinued shades, obsolete fittings; high book inventory but low cash.
operational_bottlenecks.impact: Capital locked in non-moving stock (often 15-30% of inventory), shelf space wasted, hidden margin erosion via markdowns.
operational_bottlenecks.root_cause: No SKU-level velocity tracking; reordering by gut/scheme-greed rather than data; brand-pushed stocking.

operational_bottlenecks.bottleneck: Stockouts of fast movers despite full godown
operational_bottlenecks.symptom: Contractor walks to competitor because the exact wire gauge/pipe size/shade is unavailable.
operational_bottlenecks.impact: Lost trade order plus the rest of the basket; erosion of the 'always available' reputation that drives loyalty.
operational_bottlenecks.root_cause: Inventory not managed at SKU level; reorder tied to van beat timing not actual depletion; capital trapped in dead stock.

operational_bottlenecks.bottleneck: GST and ITC leakage / reconciliation burden
operational_bottlenecks.symptom: Mismatch between GSTR-2B and purchase register; ITC blocked because supplier didn't file; cash invoices off-book.
operational_bottlenecks.impact: Lost input tax credit (real cash), notices/penalties, and over/under-payment of tax across multiple slabs.
operational_bottlenecks.root_cause: Manual or partial billing, multi-slab complexity (28% cement vs 18% paints/hardware), and non-compliant suppliers.

operational_bottlenecks.bottleneck: Pricing opacity and margin erosion under negotiation
operational_bottlenecks.symptom: Every trade buyer negotiates; counter staff give discounts without knowing true landed cost net of scheme.
operational_bottlenecks.impact: Gross margin leaks 2-5 points; profitable on paper, thin in cash after rebates are reconciled.
operational_bottlenecks.root_cause: Landed cost (net of slabs/schemes/rebates) not computed at SKU level; no price discipline tooling at the counter.

ai_automation_opportunities.opportunity: SKU-level reorder & dead-stock engine: auto-flag fast movers below reorder point and slow/dead stock for liquidation, aligned to distributor beat days.
Receivables/khata ageing automation: digitise contractor ledgers, auto WhatsApp payment reminders, credit-limit alerts and ageing buckets.
GST + ITC reconciliation bot: match GSTR-2B to purchase register, flag non-filing suppliers and blocked ITC, prep returns across slabs.
Landed-cost & dynamic counter-pricing assistant: compute true net cost after scheme/rebate, set floor prices and quote ranges for staff.
Scheme/rebate capture tracker: monitor distributor target slabs and quarterly rebates so the shop hits thresholds and claims every incentive.
Trade-customer reactivation & demand prediction: identify lapsed contractors and seasonal paint/festive demand, trigger targeted offers.

consulting_frameworks.use: Map inventory days + receivable days - payable days to expose how long cash is trapped; the single most important lens for a credit-and-stock-heavy hardware shop.
Identify the binding constraint (usually receivables/working capital or dead stock) and subordinate decisions to relieve it rather than chasing top-line.
Classify SKUs by value (A/B/C) and demand variability (X/Y/Z) to set differentiated reorder, stocking and liquidation rules across the long hardware tail.
Compute true gross margin per category net of schemes, breakage and credit cost to know which lines (paints, electricals) actually fund the shop.
Focus shelf space, credit and buying power on the ~20% of SKUs/contractors driving ~80% of cash margin; rationalise the rest.
Clarify who decides credit limits, who approves discounts, who chases recovery and who signs off purchases as the shop hires beyond family labour.

risk_model.risk: Bad debt from trade-credit/khata defaults (contractor doesn't pay or absconds)
risk_model.control: Per-customer credit limits, ageing review, partial-advance on bulk, signed delivery proof, and Sec 43B(h)-aware payment discipline; stop-supply on overdue.

risk_model.risk: GST/ITC non-compliance, multi-slab misclassification and blocked credit
risk_model.control: GST-compliant billing software, HSN-correct slabs, monthly GSTR-2B vs purchase reconciliation, e-way bills for bulk dispatch.

risk_model.risk: Dead/obsolete stock locking working capital
risk_model.control: ABC/XYZ velocity tracking, quarterly dead-stock liquidation, scheme-discipline in buying, supplier return/buyback negotiation.

risk_model.risk: Counterfeit/sub-standard goods (wires, switches, valves) and BIS non-conformance liability
risk_model.control: Source only ISI/BIS-marked electricals and pipes from authorised distributors; retain purchase invoices; avoid grey-market fast movers.

risk_model.risk: Shop establishment / labour non-compliance for counter and godown staff
risk_model.control: Shops & Establishment registration, wage/hours records, PF/ESI where applicable, professional tax registration.

risk_model.risk: Fire/safety hazard from paints, thinners, adhesives and flammable stock
risk_model.control: Segregated flammable storage, fire extinguishers, electrical load safety, local fire NOC, insurance on stock and premises.

kpi_structure.definition: COGS / average inventory at cost; how many times stock cycles to cash per year.
Average days to collect trade-credit/khata dues.
Value of SKUs with no sale in 90+ days as % of total inventory value.
(Net sales - landed COGS incl. schemes) / net sales.

kpi_structure.kpi: Fill rate / stockout on A-class SKUs
kpi_structure.definition: % of fast-mover demand served from stock without lost sale.

kpi_structure.kpi: Bad debt as % of credit sales
kpi_structure.definition: Written-off/irrecoverable dues over trailing 12 months / total credit sales.

unit_economics: Avg trade ticket ₹3,000-₹15,000 (contractor basket); walk-in homeowner ticket ₹300-₹2,500
Cement ~5-8% margin (loss-leader/footfall driver); paints 12-20%; electricals & plumbing fittings 18-30%; tools/hardware 20-35%
A Tier-2/3 single shop doing ₹3-8 cr annual turnover typically holds ₹40-90 lakh inventory and carries ₹25-60 lakh in receivables
Quarterly distributor rebates/schemes add 1-3% to effective margin when targets are hit
profitability_analysis.working_capital_notes: This is a working-capital business, not a margin business. Cash is trapped simultaneously in inventory (60-90 days) and trade receivables (30-90 days), while supplier payables run only 15-45 days, creating a negative-to-tight cash cycle. Most shops fund the gap with CC/OD limits or informal credit; the swing factor is khata recovery discipline and dead-stock liquidation. Sec 43B(h) now forces timely payment to MSME suppliers, tightening the payables float further.
levers: Cut DSO via credit limits, ageing follow-up and partial advances on bulk orders
Liquidate dead stock and use ABC/XYZ to free trapped capital and raise turns
Capture every distributor scheme/slab and buy fast movers company-direct to lift effective margin
Shift basket mix toward high-margin electricals/plumbing/tools and value-add (tinting, delivery) and away from pure cement footfall
Reduce ITC leakage and shrinkage to recover real cash already earned

playbooks.name: Stationery Chains
playbooks.one_liner: A multi-store retail chain (3-30 outlets) selling school/office stationery, notebooks, art supplies, books and gifting across Tier-2/3 Indian towns, blending walk-in retail, institutional/B2B school supply, and a seasonal demand spike around the April-June academic year.

operating_model.summary: A working-capital-heavy, low-margin, high-SKU retail format where money is made on assortment breadth, festive/academic-season velocity, private-label/gifting mix-up, and institutional bulk supply to schools and offices. The chain wins on neighbourhood density, in-stock reliability on fast-movers (notebooks, pens, exam pads), and a high-margin gifting/art tail. Profit is concentrated in a 6-8 week academic season (Apr-Jun) plus Diwali/Rakhi/wedding gifting; the rest of the year funds fixed cost.
revenue_streams: Walk-in retail: stationery, notebooks, pens, art/craft, files, calculators (bread-and-butter, ~55-65% of revenue)
Institutional / B2B supply: school stationery kits, office consumables, government/PSU tender supply, corporate diaries (bulk, lower margin, sticky)
Gifting & celebration: greeting cards, soft toys, return-gifts, festive hampers, wedding cards (highest margin, seasonal)
Books: school textbooks/guides (often publisher-locked low margin), general/competitive-exam books
Private-label & repacking: own-brand notebooks, copies, exam pads, art kits (margin uplift)
Value-added services: photocopy/print/lamination/binding, passport photo, online-form filling (high-margin footfall driver)
cost_structure: COGS / merchandise purchase (68-78% of sales) — the dominant cost; distributor and wholesale-market (e.g. Sadar Bazar Delhi, local stationery mandi) buying
Rent & CAM for high-street/near-school locations (6-12% of sales)
Store staff salaries + incentives (5-9%)
Working capital interest — inventory + institutional receivables (1-3%)
Shrinkage, damage, obsolescence (dead SKUs, dated diaries/calendars, faded cards) (1-3%)
Logistics, last-mile to institutions, packing material
Marketing/local promotion, festoons, school tie-up commissions/kickbacks
Utilities, POS/billing software, payment-gateway/UPI MDR
value_drivers: In-stock rate on the top 200 fast-movers during peak season — a stockout in May = a lost customer for the year
Assortment depth + the high-margin gifting/art/private-label tail that lifts blended margin
Institutional contracts (schools, offices, govt) that give predictable bulk volume and pre-bookable demand
Store density / neighbourhood convenience and supplier credit terms that fund the inventory

value_chain: Demand planning & seasonal forecasting (academic calendar + festive)
Assortment & range planning per store cluster
Procurement & supplier credit negotiation (distributors + wholesale mandi + publishers)
Multi-channel selling (counter retail + institutional B2B + photocopy services)

core_processes.description: Build SKU-level forecasts off prior-year sell-through + school admission trends; lock notebook/copy/textbook quantities and pre-book with distributors before the Apr-Jun rush to secure stock and credit.

Mix of distributor purchase (on 30-60 day credit) and cash buying at wholesale mandi; negotiate scheme/QPS slabs, manage Sec 43B(h) 45-day MSME supplier payment discipline, 3-way match GRN-PO-invoice.
Quote/tender for school kits & office supplies, fulfil bulk, raise GST tax invoice with e-invoice/e-way bill where applicable, then chase receivables that often run 45-90 days.
Auto-replenish fast-movers to a min-max per store, move slow stock to higher-velocity outlets, and reconcile inter-store transfers — the backbone that prevents both stockouts and dead stock.
Fast counter throughput with barcode/POS, UPI-first collection, loyalty capture, and add-on selling of photocopy/print/gifting at the counter.

department_structure.mandate: Run the stores: footfall conversion, in-stock discipline, planogram, counter throughput, shrinkage control and customer experience across outlets.
Own assortment, vendor relationships, buying terms, private-label development, pricing and markdown/liquidation calendar.
Inbound logistics, GRN, central warehouse, inter-store transfers, last-mile to institutions and inventory accuracy.
Win and service school, office, govt/PSU contracts; tendering, kit-building, bulk fulfilment and receivables follow-up.
GST filing, supplier payments (Sec 43B(h)), receivables, cash reconciliation across stores, MIS, banking and statutory compliance.
Hiring and rostering seasonal + permanent staff, payroll (EPF/ESI/PT/TDS), Shops & Establishment compliance, training.

operational_bottlenecks.bottleneck: Severe seasonal demand concentration with stockouts in peak and dead-stock off-peak
operational_bottlenecks.symptom: Top notebooks/copies/textbooks sell out by mid-May while diaries, calendars and dated gifting rot on shelves post-season
operational_bottlenecks.impact: Lost peak sales (a stockout can cost the whole-year customer), plus 1-3% of revenue locked in obsolete stock needing markdown
operational_bottlenecks.root_cause: Forecasting done on gut/last-year-photocopy rather than SKU-level sell-through and admission-trend data; long distributor lead times force a single big pre-season bet

operational_bottlenecks.bottleneck: Working capital strangled by inventory + institutional receivables
operational_bottlenecks.symptom: Cash crunch every March-April when inventory must be built but institutional dues from last term are still uncollected
operational_bottlenecks.impact: Forced cash buying loses distributor credit/scheme benefits; reliance on costly informal credit; growth stalls
operational_bottlenecks.root_cause: High-SKU inventory turns of only 3-5x, institutional DSO of 45-90 days, and weak collection discipline — the classic working-capital cash-conversion gap

operational_bottlenecks.bottleneck: Poor SKU-level inventory visibility across multiple stores
operational_bottlenecks.symptom: Same item dead in one store, stocked out in another; physical stock rarely matches the books; pilferage undetected
operational_bottlenecks.impact: Lost sales, inflated carrying cost, shrinkage of 1-3%, and inability to centrally buy with leverage
operational_bottlenecks.root_cause: Many stores still on paper/Excel or non-integrated billing; no central perpetual inventory or barcode discipline; thousands of low-value SKUs make manual tracking impossible

operational_bottlenecks.bottleneck: Margin compression on commodity stationery and publisher-locked textbooks
operational_bottlenecks.symptom: Pens, copies and prescribed textbooks sold near-MRP with razor-thin margin; online/quick-commerce undercutting on branded items
operational_bottlenecks.impact: Blended margin squeezed; net margin can fall to low single digits if mix isn't managed
operational_bottlenecks.root_cause: Commoditised fast-movers with price transparency + fixed publisher trade margins; over-dependence on low-margin SKUs vs. private-label and gifting

operational_bottlenecks.bottleneck: Heavy dependence on a few schools/institutions and informal tie-ups
operational_bottlenecks.symptom: Loss of one school contract or a kickback-driven tie-up shifting to a competitor causes a step-drop in institutional revenue
operational_bottlenecks.impact: Revenue volatility, governance/ethics risk, and pricing pressure from school managements
operational_bottlenecks.root_cause: Concentrated B2B book undocumented or relationship-only; no formal multi-year contracts or diversified institutional base

operational_bottlenecks.bottleneck: Manual GST/compliance and cash-heavy multi-store reconciliation
operational_bottlenecks.symptom: Mismatched ITC, delayed GSTR filing, daily cash from each store not tallying, e-way bills missed on institutional dispatch
operational_bottlenecks.impact: ITC loss, interest/penalties, and finance team firefighting instead of analysis
operational_bottlenecks.root_cause: Disparate billing systems, manual data entry, and owner-centric finance without integrated POS-to-accounting flow

ai_automation_opportunities.opportunity: AI seasonal demand forecasting per SKU and per store cluster off prior sell-through, school-admission and festive calendars to set pre-season buy quantities and min-max replenishment, cutting both stockouts and dead stock.
Automated multi-store replenishment and inter-store transfer suggestions that rebalance slow stock to high-velocity outlets and flag dead stock for markdown before it dates.
Institutional accounts-receivable automation: auto-ageing of school/office dues, dunning reminders, and collection prioritisation to compress DSO from 60-90 to 30-45 days.
GST automation: POS-to-GSTR reconciliation, ITC matching, e-invoice/e-way bill generation on institutional dispatch, and Sec 43B(h) supplier-payment alerts.
Supplier negotiation and procurement copilot: track distributor scheme/QPS slabs, recommend optimal buy timing/quantity, and 3-way match GRN-PO-invoice.
Assortment and pricing optimisation: identify the high-margin gifting/private-label tail to push, dynamic markdown on dated stock, and category-level mix steering to lift blended margin.
Customer/loyalty and WhatsApp re-engagement: capture buyers at counter, push pre-season notebook/kit pre-booking and gifting offers to drive repeat footfall.
Unified store MIS and CEO dashboard: daily per-store sales, margin, shrinkage and cash position with anomaly alerts for the owner.

consulting_frameworks.use: Map inventory days + institutional receivable days − supplier payable days to expose the March-April cash gap and target turns, DSO and credit terms as the primary value levers.
Treat peak-season in-stock on the top-200 fast-movers as the binding constraint; subordinate buying, warehousing and replenishment to never starving those SKUs during Apr-Jun.

Segment thousands of SKUs by value (ABC) and demand variability (XYZ) so tight control and forecasting effort go to A/X items (notebooks, pens, kits) while C/Z gifting tail is managed by simple reorder rules.
Compute per-store and per-category contribution (ticket size, gross margin, footfall conversion, basket size) to decide which categories and stores to expand, fix, or exit.
Walk buying → warehousing → store → billing → collection to find margin leakage (shrinkage, dead stock, ITC loss) and the highest-leverage automation points.
Classify categories — commodity stationery (traffic builders, low margin) vs gifting/art/private-label (profit engines) vs books (margin parasites) — to steer space, buying and promotion.
Clarify who owns buying, store in-stock, institutional collections and GST filing across a multi-store org where the founder otherwise becomes the single bottleneck.

risk_model.risk: Working-capital crunch in pre-season (inventory build collides with uncollected institutional dues)
risk_model.control: Cash-flow forecast tied to academic calendar, disciplined AR collection (DSO<45d), negotiated distributor credit and a sanctioned working-capital/CC limit kept in reserve.

risk_model.risk: Dead stock & obsolescence (dated diaries, calendars, faded cards, outdated edition textbooks)
risk_model.control: SKU-level sell-through tracking, season-end markdown calendar, conservative buying on dated items, and inter-store rebalancing before expiry of relevance.

risk_model.risk: GST non-compliance — ITC mismatch, missed e-way bills on institutional dispatch, late GSTR filing
risk_model.control: Integrated POS-to-GST reconciliation, automated e-invoice/e-way bill, monthly ITC matching and a compliance calendar with owner alerts.

risk_model.risk: Delayed payment to MSME suppliers triggering Sec 43B(h) disallowance and interest
risk_model.control: Flag MSME-registered vendors, enforce 45-day payment SLA, and reconcile payables ageing monthly against the income-tax 43B(h) deadline.

risk_model.risk: Channel disruption from online/quick-commerce undercutting on branded stationery & books
risk_model.control: Shift mix to private-label and gifting, defend institutional/service revenue (photocopy, kits), add WhatsApp/local delivery and loyalty to retain neighbourhood customers.

risk_model.risk: Over-concentration on a few school/institutional contracts (and kickback-driven, undocumented tie-ups)
risk_model.control: Diversify the institutional base, sign formal multi-year supply contracts, and codify pricing to remove governance/ethics exposure.

risk_model.risk: Inventory shrinkage and cash-handling pilferage across multiple stores
risk_model.control: Barcode/POS perpetual inventory, periodic cycle counts, CCTV, UPI-first collection to reduce cash, and exception reporting on counter voids/discounts.

risk_model.risk: Labour / establishment non-compliance on seasonal hiring (Shops Act, EPF/ESI, PT)
risk_model.control: Shops & Establishment registration per store, proper appointment letters, EPF/ESI enrolment above thresholds, and professional-tax deduction where applicable.

Share of revenue from higher-margin own-brand and gifting categories.

unit_economics: Average retail ticket: ₹120-350 walk-in (spikes to ₹800-2,500 during academic-season kit/notebook buying)
Institutional school-kit order: ₹400-1,200 per student kit at ~12-18% margin; a 600-student school = ₹3-7 lakh per term
Per-store monthly revenue (Tier-2/3): ₹4-12 lakh; gross margin ₹1-3.5 lakh; net contribution ₹25k-1 lakh after rent/staff
Photocopy/print/lamination services: ₹0.80-2 per copy at 60-75% margin — small ticket, high-margin footfall driver
Private-label notebook: bought/packed at ₹18-22, sold ₹35-45 = ~45-55% margin vs ~12-18% on branded
profitability_analysis.working_capital_notes: This is a working-capital-intensive format: inventory of ₹15-40 lakh per store turning only 3-7x, plus institutional receivables at 45-90 days, against distributor credit of only 30-60 days — creating a structural pre-season (Mar-Apr) cash gap. Cash-conversion cycle often runs 60-120 days. The single biggest profit lever is compressing this cycle: faster turns, tighter B2B collections, and maximising supplier credit/scheme benefits.
levers: Shift mix toward private-label, gifting, art and in-store services (45-75% margin) to lift blended margin
Compress institutional DSO and improve inventory turns to free trapped cash and reduce interest cost
Cut dead-stock and shrinkage through SKU-level visibility, disciplined buying and markdown timing
Negotiate distributor scheme/QPS slabs and stretch payable terms within Sec 43B(h) limits
Drive peak-season in-stock and pre-booking to capture the full Apr-Jun and festive demand

pm_workflows.initiative: Pre-season demand planning & buying cycle (academic + festive)
pm_workflows.cadence: Annual cycle with monthly reviews Dec-Jun

milestones: Identify private-label candidates (notebooks, copies, art kits)

key_activities: Plan SKU breadth/depth per store cluster
Select distributors, wholesale-mandi and publisher sources
Negotiate price, scheme/QPS slabs and credit terms
Daily sales/cash MIS and in-stock monitoring

stages.focus: Establish in-stock discipline, healthy margin mix and clean cash discipline before expanding
plays: Install POS + barcode and clean the SKU master
Build the high-margin gifting/art/private-label tail

Get GST + Shops Act + Udyam compliant and books clean

stages.focus: Centralise buying and inventory; win institutional contracts; remove founder as the single bottleneck
plays: Set up central warehouse and perpetual inventory across stores
Negotiate distributor scheme slabs on consolidated volume
Build a formal institutional/school B2B book with AR discipline
Define RACI and hire cluster/area management

stages.focus: Scale the format profitably with data-driven buying, private-label scale and omni-channel reach
plays: AI demand forecasting and auto-replenishment at SKU-store level
Scale private label as a margin engine across the chain
Add WhatsApp/online ordering, delivery and loyalty for omni-channel
Tighten working capital with banking lines and rigorous CCC management

playbooks.name: Repair / Service Businesses

ai_automation_opportunities.opportunity: AI-driven inbound triage and booking bot (WhatsApp/IVR) that captures appliance type, symptom, brand, warranty status, address pincode and auto-assigns the right technician with parts pre-picked
Predictive parts inventory: forecast fast-moving spares (compressors, PCBs, gas, motors) per region/season so technicians stop making repeat visits for want of a part
Automated job-card to GST e-invoice and digital warranty/AMC reminder flow, eliminating manual billing leakage and chasing renewals
Technician route optimisation and same-day slotting across a city beat to lift jobs-per-tech-per-day and cut travel time
First-time-fix knowledge assistant: surface model-specific repair SOPs, error-code fixes and torque/spec data to junior technicians on their phone
AMC/repeat-customer reactivation campaigns using service history to push seasonal pre-monsoon AC checks and renewal upsells
Cash-flow and technician-incentive dashboard reconciling collections vs parts cost vs payouts to plug pilferage of cash-collected jobs

consulting_frameworks.use: Link technician training/retention and tooling to first-time-fix rate, which drives customer satisfaction, repeat AMC revenue and referrals - the core flywheel of a repair business.
Identify the binding constraint (usually skilled-technician hours or parts availability), and schedule the whole operation - bookings, parts picking, routing - around protecting that constraint.
Model contribution per service job (ticket minus parts, travel, technician cost) and jobs-per-tech-per-day to know the breakeven utilisation and pricing floor for visit charges and AMCs.
Clarify who owns booking, diagnosis, parts approval, repair, QC callback and collection so jobs do not stall between call-centre, technician and back-office.
Frame the offer around the customer's real job ('get my fridge cold again fast, no repeat visits') to design SLAs, transparent quotes and AMC bundles rather than ad-hoc per-visit billing.
Manage the gap between buying spares (cash out) and OEM warranty-claim reimbursement / customer collection (cash in) - the silent killer of repair-business liquidity.

department_structure.mandate: Capture and triage all inbound (phone/WhatsApp/walk-in/online), book slots, set SLA expectations, confirm warranty status and own CSAT and re-booking
Diagnose and repair within SLA, maximise first-time-fix and jobs-per-day, manage technician beats, tools and safety
Stock fast-movers, manage OEM/aftermarket sourcing, technician van stock, warranty-part returns and pilferage control
Job-card to GST invoice, cash/UPI collection reconciliation, technician incentive payout, OEM warranty reimbursement follow-up
Acquire jobs via OEM authorisation, aggregators (UC), local SEO/Google, and convert one-time jobs to AMC contracts

Handwritten job cards and cash bills, no GST e-invoice

GST invoices raised, payments mostly UPI

OEM warranty claims reconciled systematically

digital_maturity_model.name: AI-Native Service Business
